content.p: Enniskillen was a small grey army town on the western edge of Northern Ireland, and on Sunday 8 November 1987 its people gathered, as they did every year, to remember the dead of two world wars. Shortly before 11 a.m., with crowds filling in under the wall of a building beside the cenotaph, a bomb planted by the Provisional IRA exploded. Eleven people died and 63 were injured. A twelfth victim, a headmaster named Ronnie Hill, lay in a coma for about 13 years before he died.

The attack became known as the Remembrance Day or Poppy Day bombing. It was condemned in Dublin, London and across the nationalist community, it produced a statement of forgiveness from a bereaved father that was heard around the world, and it was followed by no prosecution. Nobody was ever charged, although ten suspects were questioned, IrishCentral reports.

The bomb was left on the evening of Saturday 7 November in the St Michael's Reading Rooms, according to the Irish Times: a dilapidated building near the war memorial. The Guardian's report the next day described it as a former Catholic school that served as a community centre. It overlooked the cenotaph and was the traditional spot where civilians stood to watch the parade.

The Royal Ulster Constabulary's Chief Constable, Sir John Hermon, told reporters that the planned parade route had been searched, with sniffer dogs. The Reading Rooms had not been, because it was regarded as a secure area. The police had thought the IRA would not bomb a place used by civilians, and Hermon said the building had never been used by the security forces.

The reports differ on the size of the device. The Irish Times and IrishCentral call it a 40-pound fertiliser bomb. The Guardian's reporter, writing the day after, said 30 pounds. All agree that it brought down the building's gable wall, which the Guardian described as three storeys high, onto people standing beneath it. By the Guardian's account the square would have filled about a quarter of an hour later, when the ceremony was due. There was no warning.

Names were given as released on the day and as later listed, and spellings vary between sources. The dead included William and Agnes Mullan, Wesley and Bertha Armstrong, and Kitchener (Kit) and Jessie Johnston, three married couples. The Guardian noted that two of the husbands were elders of the Presbyterian Church. Others killed were John Megaw, a caretaker who lived in County Antrim; Georgina Quinton; Samuel Gault; a man named Armstrong; and 20-year-old nurse Marie Wilson. The Guardian called one of the dead a retired policeman, while Belfast Child described the one non-civilian among the dead as a police reservist.

The Guardian counted 19 of the 63 injured as seriously hurt. They included four children under ten and 17 teenagers, according to its tally, along with three people over 70. At least four were airlifted from the Erne Hospital for neurosurgery in Belfast and Tyrone.

Harry Donaldson, a 55-year-old lorry driver, told the Guardian from his hospital bed that he had been standing beside a pedestrian barrier. "There was a crash and the wall came down on top of us," he said. He had given Megaw a lift to the town, and Megaw, standing next to him, died. Another witness described a woman being blown through a mahogany door and surviving.
Marie Wilson died under the rubble in the arms of her father Gordon, a draper in the town, who was himself injured. He later recalled her last words as "Daddy, I love you very much".

The following morning he gave a BBC interview. Belfast Child quotes him as saying: "I bear no ill will. I bear no grudge. Dirty sort of talk is not going to bring her back to life." The Irish Times reviewer, writing in 1997, pointed out that Wilson did not say he forgave the bombers, though it is widely believed he did. He said he would pray for them, and a book by local editor Denzil McDaniel set the record straight on this.

The effect was large. After the funerals, the Irish Times reviewer wrote, loyalist retaliation was expected and did not happen; Belfast Child likewise says the paramilitaries were intent on revenge but were largely dissuaded by Wilson's words. The Irish Times reviewer credited Wilson's broadcast with part of that restraint, but wrote that the dignity of the victims' families and of the wider Protestant population mattered as well, and that Wilson alone was not responsible, as is sometimes believed. IrishCentral records that at a special Mass led by Cardinal Tomas O Fiaich in the town's Catholic church days after the bombing, the congregation of about 1,000 stood to applaud him. McDaniel, in a piece the same outlet quotes, wrote that Wilson's words were credited with helping Enniskillen hold together.

The weight of that example had a cost, too. The Irish Times review noted that relatives of other victims gradually came to feel Wilson's generosity left them no room to voice less charitable views. Belfast Child likewise says some victims did not share his sentiments and were frustrated that the media focused almost solely on him.

Wilson later became a peace campaigner and was appointed to the Seanad by Taoiseach Albert Reynolds. In 1993 he told an Irish diplomat, according to a state paper reported by the Irish Times in 2022, that he was disappointed his contacts with IRA representatives to get them to renounce violence had been futile. The same paper recorded his resentment at Ian Paisley, who had denounced him for attending a remembrance Mass at a Catholic church just after the bombing and later ignored him at an airport.

No organisation claimed the attack on the day. Sir John Hermon said he was in no doubt the IRA was responsible, and that the bomb had been placed "to murder civilians". He added that even the terrorists would be shocked by the carnage.

The IRA did address it afterwards. Belfast Child reports a statement expressing "deep regret", which also suggested the army might have set the bomb off by scanning radio frequencies. That claim was later admitted to be false, according to the same source. Hermon said that the IRA had indirectly told police that another bomb, near a cenotaph at Tullyhommon not far away, had failed to explode, and that had it gone off there would have been severe casualties. The Tullyhommon remembrance ceremony was called off. IrishCentral reports that the IRA claimed the Enniskillen bomb was aimed at British security forces at the parade and went off prematurely, and later acknowledged the attack was a mistake.

The Irish Times review of McDaniel's book records Gerry Adams admitting the bombing was a mistake, and says it disrupted the electoral strategy that he and others were promoting within republicanism. Belfast Child says Adams apologised on behalf of the republican movement in 1997. McDaniel's own view, quoted there, was that he did not believe the IRA set out specifically to kill civilians, but that it was reckless about civilian life.

The BBC says the Semtex supplied by Gaddafi's Libya was used in the Enniskillen Poppy Day bombing. The Observer reported in 2006 that about 160 people had joined a multi-million-dollar civil action against Gaddafi and Libya in a Washington court over the arming of the IRA. Twenty were victims or relatives of victims of the Enniskillen bombing; one of them, Serena Doherty, was named in the papers as having been diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder. The Observer said the suit was the largest civil case concerning terrorism in the UK. In 2021 the BBC reported that a government-commissioned report by William Shawcross on compensation for victims of Libyan-supplied weapons, delivered in May 2020, had still not been published, and that a Labour MP said the delay left victims feeling abandoned.

Belfast Child, an author's blog, adds that the bombing came after setbacks for the IRA, including the killing of eight of its members by the SAS at Loughgall and the seizure of an arms shipment from Libya, and that Libya's regime afterwards condemned the attack and withdrew support. Those claims rest on that one source.

Margaret Thatcher called the bombing a "blot on humanity" in the Guardian's words, and said angrily that no country should be left that would support those responsible. Northern Ireland Secretary Tom King called it an obscene and debased cause that required "the murder of old women and young children". In Dublin, Taoiseach Charles Haughey called it a "criminal act of carnage" and vowed to find the perpetrators. SDLP leader John Hume said the bomb was "a direct attack on the unionist community".

The Guardian noted that the SDLP's conference at the weekend had thrown out a motion saying the Irish parliament should not pass an extradition act until Britain reformed the administration of justice in Northern Ireland. After Enniskillen, the paper wrote, it seemed certain the act would go ahead.

The IrishCentral account credits the bombing with weakening public tolerance of IRA violence and helping to push talks toward the Good Friday Agreement. The Irish Times reviewer was more guarded. Enniskillen Integrated Primary School and the reconciliation group Enniskillen Together came out of the bombing, he wrote, but it did not mark the end of violence, and the media's talk of a "spirit of Enniskillen" involved wishful thinking.

Six days after the bombing an anonymous typed letter reached the Irish foreign minister, Brian Lenihan. Its writer claimed to be an MI5 agent and said British intelligence knew in advance where and when the IRA planned to plant the bomb, and had chosen to change the timing device and let it explode so the IRA would suffer a backlash. The Irish Times, reporting the letter's release in the state papers 30 years later, said it generated only one internal note, passed between two government departments. The Irish Times report offered no corroboration of the claims.

The bomb site was rebuilt. The Clinton Centre, a home for peace-building projects, opened in 2002 with former US President Bill Clinton, whose name it carries, opening it, IrishCentral says. In 2012 Queen Elizabeth visited Enniskillen, met the bereaved, and walked from the Church of Ireland cathedral into St Michael's Catholic church, the first time, IrishCentral says, that she had entered a Roman Catholic place of worship in her reign. On the 30th anniversary, in 2017, a memorial to the 12 dead was unveiled at the site, with a minute's silence exactly 30 years after the blast, and the Taoiseach, Leo Varadkar, and the Northern Ireland Secretary attended the larger commemoration that Sunday. Earlier that summer, a Sinn Fein councillor, the chair of Fermanagh and Omagh District Council, had declined to condemn the bombing, and councillors of the SDLP, UUP and DUP walked out of a later meeting in protest.
